case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the statutory 30-day deadline to file a petition for judicial review of a final removal order is a jurisdictional bar (nonwaivable and not subject to equitable tolling) or a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(1) (deadline for filing petition for review of a final order of removal).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Riley argues that § 1252(b)(1)’s 30-day filing deadline is not jurisdictional under the Supreme Court’s clear-statement framework because Congress did not clearly tie the time limit to the courts’ adjudicatory power. Therefore, the deadline should be treated as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule that can be waived or forfeited by the government and, in appropriate cases, equitably tolled—especially where strict enforcement would block review of serious legal and factual errors in removal proceedings.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Attorney General argues that the 30-day deadline in § 1252(b)(1) is jurisdictional (or must be treated as such based on the INA’s structure and the Court’s immigration-review precedent), meaning courts lack authority to hear late petitions regardless of equities. Under this view, allowing tolling or waiver would undermine Congress’s intent to impose strict, fast, and administrable limits on judicial review of removal orders.
key_precedents: Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center, 568 U.S. 145 (2013)
Hamer v. Neighborhood Housing Services of Chicago, 583 U.S. 17 (2017)
Fort Bend County v. Davis, 587 U.S. 541 (2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s statutory-stare-decisis argument from Stone is the hardest point, but Stone’s “mandatory and jurisdictional” phrasing is precisely the kind of pre-Arbaugh label Henderson and Santos-Zacaria tell us not to treat as controlling on the technical jurisdictional question, and congressional inaction cannot supply a clear statement Congress itself did not make. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right that Congress designed § 1252 for speed and finality, yet under our modern framework those structural aims support strict enforcement as a claim-processing rule rather than an implied withdrawal of adjudicatory power absent jurisdictional text. Bowles does not compel a different result because it rested on a historically entrenched notice-of-appeal regime and statutory context more explicitly tied to the court’s authority than § 1252(b)(1)’s filing-direction language. A narrow holding—nonjurisdictional but ordinarily mandatory, with equitable tolling only under traditional principles—best preserves Congress’s deadline while maintaining coherence and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s clearest point is the Court’s post-Arbaugh clear-statement line, but that atextual presumption cannot override what § 1252(b)(1) does in context: it defines the exclusive petition-for-review mechanism and makes timely filing the condition for invoking that mode of review at all. Justice Barrett’s placement argument (outside an express jurisdictional grant) does not defeat a textual reading that Congress can limit a court’s authority through operative conditions attached to the very procedure it creates, particularly in the INA’s tightly channeled scheme. Henderson and Santos-Zacaria (as Justice Sotomayor notes) properly caution against “drive-by” jurisdictional labels, yet they do not supply any textual warrant for tolling/waiver here, and Bowles reinforces that courts may not create equitable exceptions to congressionally fixed filing cutoffs that function as gateway conditions. Stone’s characterization, even if not elaborated, aligns with the best reading of the statute’s structure and the traditional treatment of appeal-like deadlines in exclusive review schemes.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s clear-statement point is the strongest counterargument: Henderson, Boechler, and Santos-Zacaria caution against treating filing directives as jurisdictional absent explicit jurisdictional terms, and they diminish the force of Stone’s pre-Arbaugh label. But in the INA’s tightly channeled, exclusive petition-for-review scheme, § 1252(b)(1)’s 30-day requirement functions as the gateway condition for invoking the court of appeals’ authority at all—akin to the traditional role of statutory appeal deadlines reinforced in Bowles, where we refused to create equitable extensions of congressionally fixed cutoffs. Justice Kavanaugh’s statutory-stare-decisis point also matters: Congress repeatedly revised § 1252’s review machinery while leaving the 30-day command untouched against the backdrop of Stone’s understanding, which strongly suggests Congress accepted that hard-stop structure for finality and administrability. Santos-Zacaria’s nonjurisdictional holding for exhaustion does not, in my view, compel treating this distinct, front-end filing deadline as waivable, because doing so risks transforming a firm statutory limit into case-by-case equitable litigation that Congress did not authorize.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s statutory-stare-decisis point—Stone’s “mandatory and jurisdictional” language plus Congress’s later amendments—remains the strongest push the other way, but under Henderson and Santos-Zacaria that kind of pre-Arbaugh label is exactly the sort of “drive-by” characterization that cannot do the jurisdictional work absent clear statutory text. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s finality and administrability concerns are real, yet they justify strict enforcement of a claim-processing rule, not an implied withdrawal of adjudicatory authority where § 1252(b)(1) is framed as a filing directive (“must be filed”) and not tied to a jurisdictional grant. Bowles does not change that analysis because, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, it arose in a distinct appellate notice-of-appeal regime with a long-settled jurisdictional tradition; importing that tradition into the INA without a clear statement would needlessly foreclose review for vulnerable noncitizens facing irreversible harm. Treating the deadline as nonjurisdictional preserves Congress’s deadline in ordinary cases while leaving room for equitable tolling only under traditional, demanding standards when fairness and access to justice so require.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s statutory-stare-decisis argument from Stone is the most serious point, but Stone’s “mandatory and jurisdictional” phrase reads like the kind of pre-Arbaugh, unelaborated label that Henderson and Santos-Zacaria instruct us not to treat as controlling on the technical jurisdictional question. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to stress finality and the INA’s tightly channeled review scheme, yet under our clear-statement approach those structural concerns cannot supply the missing textual hook tying § 1252(b)(1)’s 30-day filing directive to the court of appeals’ adjudicatory power. Bowles does not change that for me because it rested on a different statutory setting with a historically entrenched notice-of-appeal jurisdictional regime; here, the text and placement look like a mandatory claim-processing rule, enforceable strictly in ordinary cases but not jurisdictional absent clear congressional language. On a pragmatic textualist view, that classification best maintains statutory coherence with our modern jurisdictionality cases without weakening Congress’s deadline.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s statutory-stare-decisis reliance on Stone and Congress’s later amendments is the hardest point, but Henderson and Santos-Zacaria persuasively caution that pre-Arbaugh “mandatory and jurisdictional” labels are often drive-by and do not satisfy our requirement that Congress clearly tie a rule to adjudicatory power. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito rightly stress the INA’s channeling and finality interests, yet under a textualist separation-of-powers approach, structure and policy cannot do jurisdictional work the statute’s words do not do; § 1252(b)(1) reads as a filing directive (“must be filed not later than 30 days”), not a jurisdictional grant or limitation. Bowles does not compel a different result because it rested on a distinct, historically entrenched notice-of-appeal regime long understood as jurisdictional—features not shown here. Classifying the deadline as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule still allows strict enforcement in the mine-run case, without inventing an implied jurisdictional bar absent a clear textual command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s clear-statement framework and Justice Kagan’s point that § 1252(b)(1) reads like a filing directive, not an express jurisdictional grant, are the most serious challenges to my view. But Justice Thomas and Justice Alito correctly stress the INA’s tightly channeled, single-petition review scheme: the 30-day deadline functions as the gateway condition for invoking the only judicial-review mechanism Congress provided, which is historically how statutory appeal deadlines operate. Henderson and Santos-Zacaria caution against treating pre-Arbaugh labels as dispositive, yet they did not squarely overrule Stone’s specific holding that this particular deadline is “mandatory and jurisdictional,” and Congress’s repeated revision of the review provisions without changing that command reinforces the statutory-stare-decisis pull to keep Stone’s settled administrability/finality rule in place. Even if Bowles is not a perfect match, it supports the traditional understanding that congressionally fixed deadlines for invoking appellate-type review are not subject to equitable extension absent textual authorization, which counsels against recharacterizing § 1252(b)(1) in a way that invites tolling litigation in a regime built for speed and finality.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s statutory-stare-decisis argument from Stone, coupled with congressional amendments leaving § 1252(b)(1) intact, is the strongest case for treating the deadline as jurisdictional; it presses on stability in a high-volume system. But under our textualist clear-statement approach—reinforced by the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan—Stone’s pre-Arbaugh “mandatory and jurisdictional” label cannot supply the missing statutory hook: § 1252(b)(1) states only that a petition “must be filed not later than 30 days,” without speaking in jurisdictional terms or otherwise clearly tying the deadline to adjudicatory power. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s finality/administrability concerns support strict enforcement as a claim-processing rule, but they do not justify inferring a jurisdictional withdrawal absent clear text; and Bowles, as Roberts notes, rests on a distinct, historically entrenched notice-of-appeal regime with stronger jurisdictional signals than this provision. Accordingly, I remain with the Petitioner: the deadline is nonjurisdictional, though ordinarily mandatory absent waiver/forfeiture or traditional equitable tolling.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s statutory-stare-decisis argument from Stone and congressional silence is the strongest point on the other side, but Henderson and Santos-Zacaria (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress) caution that pre-Arbaugh “mandatory and jurisdictional” labels are not enough to supply the clear textual tie to adjudicatory power that our modern doctrine requires. Justice Thomas’s structural point—that § 1252(b)(1) is a gateway in a tightly channeled review scheme—persuasively supports strict enforcement in ordinary cases, yet structure and administrability cannot do the jurisdictional work Congress did not do in the text. Bowles, as Justice Barrett notes, rests on a distinct and historically entrenched notice-of-appeal regime with clearer jurisdictional signals; § 1252(b)(1) instead reads like a filing directive, so treating it as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule best preserves both Congress’s deadline and procedural fairness in exceptional cases.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under the Court’s modern clear-statement framework, a statutory time limit is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly ties it to the court’s adjudicatory authority, and § 1252(b)(1) states only that a petition for review “must be filed not later than 30 days,” without jurisdictional language. Our recent decisions treat similar deadlines as nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules absent such clarity, see Henderson v. Shinseki, 562 U.S. 428 (2011), Hamer v. Neighborhood Housing Servs., 583 U.S. 17 (2017), Fort Bend County v. Davis, 587 U.S. 541 (2019), and Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner, 596 U.S. 199 (2022); and Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, 598 U.S. 411 (2023), reinforces that immigration-review prerequisites are not jurisdictional without clear congressional direction. Stone v. INS, 514 U.S. 386 (1995), called the deadline “mandatory and jurisdictional,” but that statement was not necessary to the holding and has been described as “without elaboration,” Henderson, 562 U.S. at 437, the kind of drive-by jurisdictional label that should not override the clear-statement approach. Treating § 1252(b)(1) as a claim-processing rule preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to our current, administrable jurisdictionality doctrine while allowing equitable tolling only in extraordinary cases rather than expanding merits review wholesale.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(1) sets a firm condition on the availability of judicial review—"The petition for review must be filed not later than 30 days"—and in the immigration context Congress has tightly circumscribed federal-court review in ways that are best read as limiting the courts’ adjudicatory authority rather than merely regulating party conduct. In Stone v. INS, 514 U.S. 386, 405 (1995), this Court described the petition-for-review deadline as “mandatory and jurisdictional,” and absent a clear textual basis to treat this statutory time limit as subject to equitable exceptions, I would adhere to that understanding, consistent with the principle that statutory deadlines for invoking appellate review can be jurisdictional (Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007)). Whatever later cases say about “clear statement” and “drive-by” jurisdictional rulings, the original public meaning and structure of the INA’s review scheme indicate Congress intended a strict, administrable cutoff that courts lack authority to extend. Because the deadline is jurisdictional, it is not waivable or subject to equitable tolling.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(1) sets a firm, short deadline for seeking review of removal orders, and the INA’s overall structure reflects Congress’s aim to make immigration review swift and administrable; treating the 30-day limit as nonwaivable best effectuates that design and avoids open-ended equitable exceptions. Although Santos-Zacaria v. Garland cautioned that Stone v. INS used “jurisdictional” loosely, Stone nonetheless emphasized that timing rules governing petitions for review in immigration are “mandatory” and intended to be strictly enforced, which is consistent with the practical need for finality in removal proceedings. The Court has recognized in Bowles v. Russell that statutory appellate time limits can be jurisdictional, and here the petition-for-review mechanism functions as the exclusive avenue for judicial review, making strict enforcement especially appropriate. Allowing waiver or equitable tolling would invite satellite litigation over excuses and materially undermine Congress’s chosen 30-day cutoff in § 1252(b)(1).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline lacks the clear jurisdictional statement this Court now requires, because it does not speak in jurisdictional terms or expressly tie timeliness to the court of appeals’ adjudicatory power. Under Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., Henderson v. Shinseki, and Boechler, absent that clear statement the deadline is a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule, which may be waived/forfeited and is presumptively subject to equitable tolling where fairness so requires. Stone v. INS’s description of the deadline as “mandatory and jurisdictional” was, as Henderson noted, “without elaboration” and thus resembles the kind of drive-by jurisdictional label the Court has since disfavored; Santos-Zacaria further cautions against reading Stone as using “jurisdictional” in today’s strict sense. Treating § 1252(b)(1) as nonjurisdictional better preserves meaningful access to judicial review in removal cases—where the stakes include exile and family separation—while still allowing courts to enforce timeliness absent equitable circumstances.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under this Court’s clear-statement framework, a time limit is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly ties it to the court’s adjudicatory power; § 1252(b)(1) sets a filing deadline but does not speak in jurisdictional terms or locate the limit in a jurisdiction-granting provision. Stone v. INS’s description of the predecessor deadline as “mandatory and jurisdictional,” 514 U.S. at 405, was a passing, pre-Arbaugh remark not essential to the holding and thus cannot override the modern rule that courts should not treat procedural prescriptions as jurisdictional absent clarity. Consistent with Henderson, Wong, and Boechler, the better reading is that § 1252(b)(1) is a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule—still strict and ordinarily enforced, but subject to waiver/forfeiture and equitable tolling in appropriate cases. That approach preserves administrable deadlines while avoiding the needless, nontextual consequence of depriving courts of authority when Congress has not clearly said so.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under this Court’s clear-statement framework, a statutory limit is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly ties it to the court’s adjudicatory power; § 1252(b)(1) states only that a petition “must be filed not later than 30 days,” without jurisdictional language or placement in a jurisdiction-granting provision. As in Boechler and Santos-Zacaria, that absence of a clear jurisdictional command means the deadline is a mandatory claim-processing rule, presumptively subject to waiver/forfeiture and (where consistent with the statute) equitable tolling. Stone’s earlier description of an INA deadline as “mandatory and jurisdictional” cannot control after our modern doctrine because it did not attend to today’s jurisdictional distinction and the point was not central to the case. Treating § 1252(b)(1) as nonjurisdictional better respects separation-of-powers limits by enforcing Congress’s text as written, rather than converting a filing rule into an implied withdrawal of judicial power.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(1) sets a statutory 30-day deadline for petitions for review, and in Stone v. INS the Court characterized the immigration petition-for-review deadline as “mandatory and jurisdictional,” a construction Congress has left undisturbed through subsequent amendments—considerations that ordinarily carry significant weight under statutory stare decisis. Although the Court’s later clear-statement cases (Arbaugh, Henderson, Hamer, Fort Bend, Boechler, Santos-Zacaria) caution against treating procedural requirements as jurisdictional absent clear congressional language, none has expressly overruled Stone’s specific treatment of the INA deadline, and the immigration review scheme’s emphasis on speed and administrability supports a strict, nonwaivable rule. As a practical matter, allowing equitable tolling or waiver in this context risks uncertainty and satellite litigation over timeliness in a system Congress designed to be streamlined. Given the Court’s institutional interest in stability and Congress’s evident design in § 1252(b)(1), I would adhere to Stone unless and until the Court squarely revisits it.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the Court’s clear-statement framework, § 1252(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly conditions the court of appeals’ adjudicatory authority on timely filing, and the text does not do so. Like the exhaustion requirement in the same review scheme, § 1252(d)(1), which we held nonjurisdictional in Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, § 1252(b)(1) lacks jurisdictional language and instead reads as a filing directive—typical of claim-processing rules. Stone v. INS’s statement that the deadline is “mandatory and jurisdictional” was made without analysis and did not control the outcome, and our later cases caution against treating such “drive-by” characterizations as dispositive when they conflict with the modern clear-statement approach (Henderson; Fort Bend; Boechler). Treating § 1252(b)(1) as nonjurisdictional respects the statutory text while leaving room for waiver/forfeiture and (where the statute permits) equitable tolling consistent with United States v. Wong.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under this Court’s clear-statement framework, § 1252(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline should be treated as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule because Congress did not clearly tie the time limit to the courts’ adjudicatory power. See Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., Henderson v. Shinseki, and Boechler (requiring a clear jurisdictional statement and rejecting jurisdictional characterization absent that clarity). Stone v. INS’s “mandatory and jurisdictional” phrasing was a passing, non-essential statement—what Henderson described as “without elaboration”—and thus does not control against the Court’s modern approach; treating the deadline as nonjurisdictional better protects procedural fairness by allowing waiver/forfeiture and equitable tolling in exceptional cases without negating the statute’s general administrability. This approach is consistent with Santos-Zacaria’s instruction to police jurisdiction carefully and avoid converting procedural requirements into nonwaivable bars without clear congressional command.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the statutory deadline to file a petition for review of a removal order in federal court is jurisdictional (thus not subject to equitable tolling) or a nonjurisdictional claims-processing rule that can be tolled in appropriate circumstances.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(1) (the 30-day deadline to file a petition for review of a final order of removal).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Riley argues that § 1252(b)(1)’s 30-day filing deadline is not jurisdictional because Congress did not clearly state that it limits the courts’ subject-matter jurisdiction. Under the Supreme Court’s modern 'clear statement' framework distinguishing jurisdictional rules from claims-processing rules, the deadline should be treated as a nonjurisdictional filing rule and therefore subject to equitable tolling (at least in extraordinary circumstances), especially given the high stakes of removal and the need for meaningful judicial review.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Attorney General argues that § 1252(b)(1)’s 30-day deadline should be treated as jurisdictional (or at least as a strict, non-tollable limit) based on the INA’s structure, the longstanding treatment of petition-for-review deadlines as mandatory, and the need for finality and administrability in immigration proceedings. On this view, untimely petitions must be dismissed without reaching equitable exceptions because the court lacks power to hear them.
key_precedents: Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center, 568 U.S. 145 (2013)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett make the strongest case that our post-Arbaugh clear-statement framework (as reinforced by Santos-Zacaria) cautions against treating older “jurisdictional” phrasing as dispositive where the statute lacks explicit jurisdictional terms. But Stone is not merely a drive-by label; it squarely construed this specific INA petition-for-review deadline in the very appellate-review posture at issue, and that construction has anchored decades of immigration-review practice—making statutory stare decisis and congressional reenactment after multiple INA amendments unusually weighty here. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Henderson/Wong and the agency-to-court distinction from Bowles is significant, yet it does not supply a clearer textual signal that Congress authorized equitable tolling in § 1252(b)(1) or that we have repudiated Stone as to this particular provision. Under a minimalist, institution-protective approach, the narrower course is to adhere to the settled rule and leave any equitable safety valve to Congress rather than recast this entrenched deadline through our later jurisdictionality vocabulary.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press that Arbaugh/Henderson/Boechler/Santos-Zacaria require a clear textual jurisdictional statement and discount Stone as pre-modern “drive-by” usage, but Stone is not merely a label—it construed this very INA petition-for-review deadline within Congress’s carefully reticulated, appellate-like review scheme and treated timely filing as a condition on the court’s authority to entertain the petition. Even accepting Santos-Zacaria’s caution about imprecise terminology, it does not justify discarding Stone’s specific construction of § 1252(b)(1) where the text (“must be filed not later than 30 days”) functions as the gateway to the statutory grant of review and where Congress has repeatedly amended the INA against that settled backdrop. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Wong and equitable tolling in some agency contexts cannot overcome the INA’s distinctive structure and Congress’s evident choice of a short, rigid deadline to promote finality; Bowles underscores that courts may not create equitable exceptions to congressionally fixed time limits for invoking appellate-type review. Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory stare decisis point further confirms that, absent a clear repudiation by Congress or this Court of Stone as applied to § 1252(b)(1), we should not recharacterize this deadline to permit tolling.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan press the clear-statement line (Arbaugh, Henderson, Boechler, Santos-Zacaria) and emphasize that § 1252(b)(1) lacks explicit jurisdictional words and that Stone’s “mandatory and jurisdictional” phrasing could be pre-Arbaugh imprecision. But Stone is not a mere label here: it addressed this specific petition-for-review deadline within the INA’s tightly reticulated review scheme, where the 30-day limit functions as a condition on the statutory grant of review and has generated substantial reliance, as the Chief underscores. Justice Jackson’s attempt to confine Bowles to Article III-to-Article III appeals does not persuade me because the operative principle is judicial inability to craft equitable exceptions to congressionally fixed, short deadlines for invoking appellate-type review, even when the decisionmaker below is an agency. Equity and harsh-case concerns (Justice Sotomayor) are real, but under a textualist and consequence-attentive approach they do not justify importing tolling into a scheme Congress designed for prompt finality absent a clearer textual signal.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory-stare-decisis argument grounded in Stone is the hardest counterweight because it reflects decades of immigration practice and a plausible congressional-reenactment story. But under our modern clear-statement framework (Henderson, Boechler, Santos-Zacaria), Stone’s pre-Arbaugh “mandatory and jurisdictional” label cannot substitute for Congress’s own unmistakable jurisdictional text—especially where § 1252 elsewhere uses explicitly jurisdictional language and § 1252(b)(1) does not. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Bowles does not move me because Bowles involved a historically jurisdictional Article III appeal deadline, while this agency-to-court scheme fits the line of cases presuming nonjurisdictionality and allowing equitable tolling only in extraordinary circumstances (Wong). Justice Alito’s finality and administrability concerns argue for strict claims-processing enforcement, not for transforming an unadorned deadline into a jurisdictional trap that most harms vulnerable noncitizens without a clear congressional command.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s statutory stare decisis point—Stone’s specific “mandatory and jurisdictional” treatment of this very deadline and Congress’s later amendments without altering the 30-day text—carries real institutional weight, and I take Justice Roberts’s reliance concerns seriously. But under our post-Arbaugh clear-statement framework, as Justice Barrett emphasizes, we do not let a pre-modern jurisdictional label substitute for Congress’s own jurisdictional words, and Santos-Zacaria specifically warns against freezing drive-by usage into jurisdictional doctrine. Justice Thomas and Justice Alito lean on Bowles and finality, but Bowles involved an Article III appellate deadline with a distinct pedigree; in this agency-to-court scheme, Henderson/Wong/Boechler push us to treat the 30-day rule as a mandatory claims-processing rule unless the statute unmistakably ties it to adjudicatory power. Congress’s ability to use explicit jurisdictional language elsewhere in § 1252 makes its silence here especially telling, and strict enforcement plus limited equitable tolling can protect administrability without overreading the text.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s best point is statutory stare decisis: as he notes, Stone spoke directly to this deadline and Congress later amended the INA without changing the 30-day language. But under our post-Arbaugh framework—emphasized by Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan—we require Congress to clearly state when a rule is jurisdictional, and § 1252(b)(1) lacks that language while adjacent provisions in § 1252 show Congress knows how to speak in jurisdictional terms. Justice Thomas’s Bowles analogy does not dislodge that conclusion because Bowles rested on a historically jurisdictional Article III appeal deadline; here, in an agency-to-court review scheme, Henderson, Wong, Boechler, and Santos-Zacaria counsel that old “mandatory and jurisdictional” labels and congressional silence are too slender to strip courts of power. Justice Alito’s finality and administrability concerns are real, but they support strict enforcement of a claims-processing rule—not transforming an unadorned deadline into a jurisdictional bar without Congress’s unmistakable command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory stare decisis argument grounded in Stone and congressional amendments is the most serious institutional counterweight, and I agree it counsels caution about unsettling immigration practice. But under Arbaugh/Henderson/Boechler/Santos-Zacaria, we cannot treat Stone’s pre-clear-statement “mandatory and jurisdictional” label plus congressional silence as a substitute for jurisdictional text—especially where § 1252 elsewhere uses expressly jurisdictional language and § 1252(b)(1) does not. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on Bowles does not move me because Bowles involved a historically jurisdictional Article III appellate deadline; in this agency-to-court petition-for-review setting, our modern framework presumes nonjurisdictionality absent a clear statement while still permitting strict claims-processing enforcement and only extraordinary equitable tolling. On an institutionalist conservative approach, the legitimacy-protecting course is to apply our clarified jurisdictionality doctrine faithfully rather than perpetuate imprecise older terminology that expands jurisdiction beyond Congress’s clear command.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory stare decisis and reenactment argument is the most substantial counterweight because Stone has long shaped immigration practice, but under our modern clear-statement rule we look first to what Congress enacted, not to a pre-Arbaugh jurisdictional label in our own opinions. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 1252(b)(1) lacks jurisdictional language while neighboring provisions in § 1252 show Congress knows how to speak in unmistakably jurisdictional terms, which cuts strongly against treating the 30-day limit as a limit on adjudicatory power. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Bowles does not move me because that case involved an Article III appellate deadline with a distinct historical pedigree, whereas this agency-to-court petition-for-review scheme fits Henderson/Boechler/Santos-Zacaria’s presumption against jurisdictional time bars absent clear text. Justice Alito’s finality and administrability concerns are real, but they are addressed by strict enforcement of a mandatory claims-processing rule with tolling (if available at all) confined to extraordinary circumstances rather than by expanding jurisdictional forfeitures beyond what the statute clearly says.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory-stare-decisis and congressional-reenactment argument remains the most serious counterweight, because Stone has structured immigration practice for decades. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, our post-Arbaugh clear-statement framework (reinforced in Santos-Zacaria) treats pre-modern “mandatory and jurisdictional” labels as insufficient to supply the jurisdictional consequence absent clear jurisdictional text, and § 1252(b)(1) conspicuously lacks the kind of jurisdictional language Congress used elsewhere in § 1252. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on Bowles underscores finality and administrability concerns, but Bowles’s Article III appellate pedigree—and the principle that consequences cannot create jurisdiction where Congress didn’t clearly speak—makes it an imperfect fit here; those concerns are better handled by strict claims-processing enforcement with equitable tolling only in truly extraordinary cases. Congressional silence after Stone does not overcome the absence of a clear jurisdictional statement in the statute itself under our clarified doctrine.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(1) sets a short, fixed 30-day period to seek judicial review of a final removal order, and in Stone v. INS this Court expressly characterized the materially identical petition-for-review deadline as “mandatory and jurisdictional,” a construction that has structured immigration review for decades. While our later cases (Arbaugh, Henderson, Wong, Boechler, Santos-Zacaria) apply a clear-statement approach and have narrowed the category of jurisdictional rules, statutory stare decisis counsels caution in treating Stone’s specific holding on this very deadline as implicitly overruled, particularly given Congress’s repeated amendments to the INA without altering the deadline’s operative language. A narrow, institutionally stabilizing resolution is to adhere to Stone unless and until Congress clearly provides otherwise, thereby preserving administrability and finality in removal proceedings consistent with the INA’s structure. On that basis, the deadline should be treated as jurisdictional and not subject to equitable tolling.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(1) provides that a petition for review “must be filed not later than 30 days” after the final order of removal, and that fixed deadline is best read as a condition on the statutory grant of review rather than a freestanding, judge-adjustable claims-processing rule. In Stone v. INS, 514 U.S. 386, 405 (1995), this Court treated the INA’s petition-for-review deadline as “mandatory and jurisdictional,” and I would adhere to that understanding absent clear textual authorization for equitable tolling, especially in a context where Congress has carefully limited judicial review in § 1252. Although cases like Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006), and Santos-Zacaria v. Garland, 598 U.S. 411 (2023), emphasize a “clear statement” approach, they do not justify rewriting a congressionally imposed, short and specific filing window that functions as a limit on the courts’ power to entertain late petitions. Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), reinforces that when Congress sets a statutory time to invoke appellate-type review, courts lack authority to create equitable exceptions.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(1) sets a firm 30-day deadline for seeking judicial review of a removal order, and the INA’s overall structure reflects Congress’s strong interest in prompt, administrable, and final resolution of removal proceedings—interests that are undermined if equitable tolling becomes a routine backstop. In Stone v. INS, 514 U.S. 386, 405 (1995), this Court described the petition-for-review deadline as “mandatory and jurisdictional,” and even if later cases have narrowed how much weight to give such characterizations, the immigration context still counsels against importing flexible tolling absent a clear statutory signal. Unlike remedial schemes where this Court has been more willing to treat deadlines as nonjurisdictional, see United States v.
